title: Why do Jupiter's poles glow?
objectives: Follow the chain from the metallic hydrogen ocean to the aurora.
See that the magnetic field and the weather have different sources.

steps.caption: This is a simplified model of Jupiter. It is a teaching model: the layers are approximate, and nobody has seen the interior directly. Press Explode to open it up, or pinch with both hands and pull apart.
steps.hint: Press Explode. You can also pinch with both hands and pull them apart.

steps.caption: Press Trace to follow the electric currents from the metallic hydrogen ocean to the glowing poles.
steps.hint: The Trace button is in the panel next to you.

steps.caption: Stop the dynamo: unplug the link between the metallic hydrogen ocean and the magnetic field.
steps.hint: Select the highlighted link, then press Unplug.

on_enter.text: Currents here are thought to make the field.

steps.caption: Before you look: point at the first part that loses what it needs.
steps.hint: Which part does a dynamo make?

on_enter.question: Which part loses its source first?

feedback.correct: Right. With no dynamo there is no magnetic field, so nothing steers charged particles to the poles and the aurora fades.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. The magnetic field loses its source first. Without it nothing steers charged particles to the poles, so the aurora fades.

steps.caption: The field and the aurora are gone, but the storms keep turning: the weather runs on heat from below, not on the magnetic field. This is the teaching model's rule, not an observation of Jupiter.
Plug the link back into the right socket.
steps.hint: The link came from the metallic hydrogen ocean. Which part does a dynamo make?

steps.caption: The poles glow again. Press Collapse to close the planet up, or push your hands together.
steps.hint: Press Collapse. You can also bring your hands together.
